title: "Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/09-rmarkdown/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](09-rmarkdown-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

You have code that calculates growth and draws a figure. How do you hand that to
someone as a readable report, without copying numbers and pictures into a Word
file by hand, where they go out of date as soon as the data change? An
**R Markdown report** is one file, ending in `.Rmd`, that holds your text and your
R code. **Rendering** it runs the code and produces an HTML page with the text,
the results and the figures together. When the data change, you render again.

(These course webpages are made with Quarto, a close relative. You only need
R Markdown.)

**Save today:** `report.Rmd` and its rendered HTML.

## The report template

Open the project and click `report.Rmd` in the Files pane. Keep it in the project
folder, next to `data/`, so that `data/seedlings.csv` still points to the data;
moved into `reports/`, the same path would point to a folder that does not exist.

A minimal report looks like this:

<pre><code>---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

&#96;&#96;&#96;{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings &lt;- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings &lt;- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
&#96;&#96;&#96;

There are &#96;r nrow(seedlings)&#96; plants in the dataset.

&#96;&#96;&#96;{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
&#96;&#96;&#96;

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.
</code></pre>

It has three kinds of content. The **header**, between the two `---` lines, sets
the title and says the output is an HTML page. Ordinary **text** is written as is;
`## Question` makes a heading. A **code chunk** starts with three backticks and
`{r}` and ends with three backticks; the word after `r`, such as `import`, is the
chunk's **label**, and every label must be different. The sentence with
<code>&#96;r nrow(seedlings)&#96;</code> is **inline code**: when the report is rendered, R
replaces it with the number of plants, 24.

A `#` means different things in the two places: in the text it makes a heading,
inside a chunk it starts an R comment.

## Rendering the report

Save the file and click **Knit**. R starts a fresh session, runs the chunks from
top to bottom, and writes an HTML page that opens in a viewer. You can do the
same from the **Console**:

```{r}
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
```

`rmarkdown::render` uses the `render()` function from the `rmarkdown` package.
`output_dir = "reports"` puts the HTML in `reports/`; the `.Rmd` stays where it
is. Knit may put the HTML next to the `.Rmd` instead, so look for the file rather
than assuming where it went. Never put the render line inside the report itself:
the report would try to render itself.

Because rendering starts fresh, the report must contain every step it needs:
`library()` lines, the import and the calculations. Something you only typed in
the Console does not exist when the report is rendered.

## A figure with a caption

Load `ggplot2` in the first chunk, and add the growth plot from day 8 in its own
chunk. `fig.cap` gives the figure a caption:

<pre><code>&#96;&#96;&#96;{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point is one independently potted seedling."}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)")
&#96;&#96;&#96;
</code></pre>

The caption says what the figure shows. Below it, write a sentence saying what
you see, for example that growth varies within both groups and the groups
overlap.

## Your first report

1. Render the supplied template before changing anything, to find out whether
   your setup works. An HTML page should open. If it does not, fix that first.
2. Change the title and the question to your own words and render again.
3. Put the import, the growth calculation and the labelled growth figure in
   chunks, in that order. If the template creates the same object twice, keep
   one.
4. Write a short methods paragraph: what one row is (one plant), how growth was
   calculated, and in which unit.
5. Misspell a column name on purpose, e.g. `growth_m`, and render. Find the
   chunk label in the error message, fix the spelling, and render again.
6. Restart R (**Session → Restart R**) and render once more. It works, because
   the report contains every step it needs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: rendering stops

Read the first error and the chunk label it names. Is the package loaded with
`library()` before its functions are used? Are the data imported before the
calculation? Are the file and column names spelt exactly? Does every chunk have
an opening and a closing fence? When you ask for help, include the error text.
:::

## When rendering stops

Errors are easier to fix once you have seen them on purpose. Save a copy of your
report as `report-workshop.Rmd`, in the project folder, and break it in three
ways, one at a time. Each time, note in `reports/render-recovery.txt` what you
changed, the first line of the error, and how you fixed it; then fix it and
render again before the next break.

1. Give two chunks the same label to find out what R says. It stops with a
   message about a **duplicate chunk label** and names the label.
2. Misspell the CSV file name in the import, e.g. `data/seedling.csv`, to find out
   what a missing input looks like. The error says the file **does not exist**.
   An object of the same name left in your Console does not help, because
   rendering starts fresh.
3. Move the plot chunk above the chunk that calculates `growth_mm`. The error says
   `growth_mm` (or `seedlings`) was **not found**: chunks run from top to bottom,
   so a figure can only use what earlier chunks made.

Finally, open the HTML in a browser next to the `.Rmd`. The `.Rmd` is the recipe
you edit; the HTML is the reading copy, and changes made to it are lost at the
next render. The measurements themselves are in `data/seedlings.csv`.

## A report for the second class's data

Use **Save As** to make `transfer-report.Rmd`, in the project folder, for the
18-plant study in `data/seedlings-transfer.csv`. The point is a report that
describes that study and nothing else.

1. Change the import to `data/seedlings-transfer.csv` and call the table
   `transfer`. Keep the `library()` lines and the growth calculation in the report.
2. Use inline code to state the number of plants, so the report itself finds out
   how many there are. The HTML should say **18**.
3. Rewrite the question, methods and caption for this study: 18 plants, 9 per
   group. Add the growth-by-group figure and the initial-versus-final figure from
   `day08-transfer.R`, each with a caption saying what one point is and what the
   y-axis measures.
4. Restart R and render. Then search the `.Rmd` for `24` and for `seedlings.csv`.
   Every hit is a sentence or line that may still describe the other study; fix
   any that do.
5. Find out whether the report works in another place: copy
   `transfer-report.Rmd`, `introcomputing.Rproj`, the `data` folder and empty
   `output` and `reports` folders into a new practice folder, open that copy's
   `.Rproj` and render there. If something is missing, note it in
   `render-recovery.txt`.

The finished transfer report describes 18 plants, 9 per group, none missing, and
T01 grew 15.0 mm.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: the HTML still says 24

A number typed into the text does not change when the data change. Replace it
with inline code such as <code>&#96;r nrow(transfer)&#96;</code>, and check that the import really
reads the transfer file.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Which files do you keep?

The `.Rmd` source, its input data and the HTML. The HTML is convenient to read,
but only the `.Rmd` can make it again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why not just type the number of plants into the sentence?

A typed number stays the same when the data change. Inline code recalculates it
at every render.
:::

**Keep:** your saved `report.Rmd` and a successfully rendered HTML report.
